los.text: Describe the signs, symptoms and complications of patients presenting with type 2 diabetes
los.html:
Often asymptomatic (found on screening/routine bloods); ~1 in 3 undiagnosed for years.
Hyperglycaemic symptomsPolyuria, polydipsia, nocturia, fatigue, blurred vision, weight loss (less than T1DM), recurrent infections (thrush, UTIs, skin infections), slow wound healing.
SignsObesity (central), acanthosis nigricans, hypertension; signs of complications.
Complications
  • Macrovascular: CHD, stroke, peripheral arterial disease.
  • Microvascular: retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy.
  • Diabetic foot: ulcers, Charcot foot, infection, amputation.
  • Acute: HHS, hypoglycaemia (treatment-related), DKA (less common).
  • Other: erectile dysfunction, gastroparesis, MASLD, periodontal disease, depression, cognitive decline, ↑ infection, cataracts.
Risk factorsObesity, inactivity, FHx, South Asian, Black African/Caribbean ethnicity, age, previous GDM, PCOS, prediabetes, metabolic syndrome, antipsychotics/steroids.

los.text: Describe the pathophysiology, diagnosis and investigations of type 2 diabetes mellitus
sessions: Clin 2: Pathophysiology and diagnosis of T2DM
los.html:
Pathophysiology
  • Insulin resistance (liver: ↑ gluconeogenesis; muscle: ↓ GLUT4 uptake; adipose: ↑ lipolysis → ↑ free fatty acids → lipotoxicity) + progressive β-cell dysfunction/failure (glucotoxicity, lipotoxicity, amylin deposition, genetics).
  • Also ↓ incretin effect, ↑ glucagon, ↑ renal glucose reabsorption (SGLT2), CNS appetite dysregulation ("ominous octet").
  • Central adiposity is the main driver
  • Residual insulin prevents ketosis.
Diagnosis (WHO)
TestDiabetesPrediabetes (non-diabetic hyperglycaemia)
HbA1c≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%)42–47
Fasting glucose≥7.0 mmol/L6.1–6.9 (IFG)
Random glucose≥11.1 with symptoms—
2 h OGTT≥11.17.8–11.0 (IGT)
AsymptomaticNeed two abnormal results (repeat test). Symptomatic → one is enough.
HbA1c unreliableHaemoglobinopathies, anaemia (iron deficiency ↑, haemolysis ↓), pregnancy, children, CKD, recent transfusion, rapid-onset diabetes (T1DM).
Baseline/annual investigationsHbA1c, lipids, U&E/eGFR + urine ACR, LFTs, BP, BMI, retinal screening, foot check, CV risk.
Consider other typesT1DM/LADA (young, slim, ketosis, rapid weight loss → GAD/islet antibodies, C-peptide), MODY (FHx, young), pancreatic (type 3c).

los.text: Describe the principles of treatment and management of type 2 diabetes mellitus (include lifestyle)
sessions: Clin 3: Principles of treatment and management of T2DM
los.html:
Structured education (DESMOND in England; X-PERT; local programmes in Wales) at diagnosis.
Lifestyle
  • Weight loss (10–15 kg can induce remission, e.g. DiRECT with low-calorie total diet replacement)
  • Healthy diet (↓ refined carbohydrates, high fibre)
  • ≥150 min/week activity
  • Smoking cessation
  • Alcohol moderation.
Individualised HbA1c targets
  • 48 mmol/mol on lifestyle ± single drug not causing hypoglycaemia
  • 53 on drugs that can cause hypoglycaemia or dual therapy
  • Relax in frail/elderly/limited life expectancy.
  • Intensify if ≥58.
Drug pathway (NICE NG28)
  • Metformin first line (modified-release if GI intolerance).
  • Add SGLT2 inhibitor if heart failure, established CVD or high CV risk (QRISK ≥10%), and with CKD.
  • Then dual/triple therapy (DPP-4i, pioglitazone, sulfonylurea, SGLT2i)
  • GLP-1 RA if BMI ≥35 or intolerant of insulin
  • Insulin (basal NPH/long-acting first) when needed.
CV risk reductionStatin (atorvastatin 20 mg primary prevention if QRISK ≥10%; 80 mg secondary), BP control (<140/90; ACEi/ARB first line regardless of age/ethnicity), antiplatelet only for established CVD.
RenalACEi/ARB if ACR >3; SGLT2i.
Annual review ("9 care processes")HbA1c, BP, cholesterol, creatinine, urine ACR, foot check, BMI, smoking status, (+ retinal screening).
Sick day rulesPause metformin, SGLT2i, ACEi/ARB, diuretics, NSAIDs when dehydrated/acutely unwell ("SADMANS").
DrivingInform DVLA if on insulin; check glucose before driving if on sulfonylurea/insulin.

los.text: Explain the macrovascular complications of diabetes mellitus
los.html:
Macrovascular diseaseAccelerated atherosclerosis of large/medium arteries; CVD is the main cause of death in T2DM (risk ×2–4).
Mechanisms
  • Hyperglycaemia → advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) → cross-link proteins, RAGE activation → inflammation, oxidative stress
  • Endothelial dysfunction (↓ NO)
  • Dyslipidaemia (↑ TG, ↓ HDL, small dense LDL)
  • Hypertension
  • Insulin resistance/hyperinsulinaemia
  • ↑ platelet aggregation and hypercoagulability (↑ PAI-1, fibrinogen)
  • Chronic inflammation
  • Smoking/obesity clustering.
Manifestations
  • Coronary heart disease: angina, MI (often silent/atypical due to autonomic neuropathy), heart failure (+ diabetic cardiomyopathy).
  • Cerebrovascular: ischaemic stroke, TIA, vascular dementia.
  • Peripheral arterial disease: claudication, critical limb ischaemia, gangrene; combined with neuropathy → diabetic foot and amputation.
  • Renal artery stenosis.
Prevention
  • Control BP, lipids (statin), glucose, smoking cessation, weight loss, exercise
  • SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs reduce CV events (cardiorenal benefits beyond glucose lowering)
  • Aspirin for secondary prevention.
  • Multifactorial intervention (STENO-2) halves CV events.

los.text: Describe the hormonal control of blood glucose levels and describe the main types of diabetes mellitus
los.html:
Insulin(β cells)
  • Released when glucose enters via GLUT2
  • → glucokinase
  • → ↑ ATP
  • → K_ATP channels close
  • → depolarisation
  • → Ca²⁺ influx
  • → insulin exocytosis (biphasic).
  • Also stimulated by amino acids, incretins (GLP-1, GIP), vagus.
  • Actions (anabolic): ↑ glucose uptake into muscle and fat (GLUT4 translocation), ↑ glycogenesis, ↑ lipogenesis, ↑ protein synthesis
  • ↓ gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis, ketogenesis
  • Drives K⁺ into cells.
Glucagon(α cells)Released with hypoglycaemia/fasting, amino acids, sympathetic stimulation; ↑ glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, ketogenesis (liver).
Counter-regulatory hormonesAdrenaline (rapid), cortisol, GH (slower) → raise glucose. Somatostatin inhibits both insulin and glucagon.
Normal fasting glucose4–6 mmol/L.
TypeMechanismFeatures
Type 1Autoimmune β-cell destruction (GAD, IA-2, ZnT8 antibodies) → absolute insulin deficiencyChildren/young adults (any age), slim, weight loss, DKA, insulin-dependent
Type 2Insulin resistance + relative deficiency~90%; adults (increasingly young), obesity, gradual
GestationalPregnancy insulin resistanceResolves postpartum; ↑ future T2DM
MODYMonogenic (HNF1A, GCK), ADYoung, FHx, non-obese; HNF1A responds to sulfonylureas
SecondaryPancreatic (pancreatitis, CF, pancreatectomy, haemochromatosis), endocrine (Cushing's, acromegaly), drugs (steroids, antipsychotics)
LADASlow autoimmuneAdults, antibodies positive

los.text: Describe the acute complications of type 2 diabetes mellitus
sessions: BMS 2: Acute complications of diabetes mellitus
los.html:
Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS)

Typically elderly T2DM; develops over days; precipitated by infection, MI, stroke, steroids, dehydration.
Features
  • Severe dehydration, glucose usually >30 mmol/L, osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, no significant ketosis (ketones <3) or acidosis (pH >7.3, HCO₃⁻ >15)
  • Confusion/↓ GCS, seizures
  • High VTE risk.
PathophysiologyEnough insulin to suppress ketogenesis but not hyperglycaemia → osmotic diuresis → severe fluid loss (~100–200 mL/kg).
Rx
  • IV 0.9% saline (slow, careful correction: aim fall in Na⁺ ≤10 mmol/L/24 h and glucose ≤5 mmol/L/h), monitor osmolality
  • Insulin (low dose 0.05 units/kg/h) only once glucose stops falling with fluids (or if ketonaemic)
  • Replace K⁺
  • LMWH prophylaxis
  • Treat cause.

Hypoglycaemia (<4 mmol/L)

Caused by sulfonylureas and insulin; missed meals, exercise, alcohol, renal impairment.
SymptomsAutonomic (sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger) → neuroglycopenic (confusion, drowsiness, odd behaviour, seizures, coma). Hypoglycaemia unawareness with long duration/β-blockers.
Rx
  • Conscious → 15–20 g fast-acting carbohydrate (e.g. glucose tablets/juice), recheck in 15 min, then long-acting carbohydrate.
  • Unconscious/unable to swallow → IV glucose (e.g. 10% 150–200 mL) or IM glucagon 1 mg.

DKA in T2DM

  • Can occur (severe illness, SGLT2 inhibitors → euglycaemic DKA, ketosis-prone T2DM).

los.text: Describe the microvascular complications of diabetes mellitus
sessions: BMS 3: Microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus overview
los.html:
• Mechanisms: chronic hyperglycaemia
    • → polyol pathway (aldose reductase: glucose → sorbitol → osmotic damage), AGEs, PKC activation, oxidative stress, hexosamine pathway
    • → microvascular basement membrane thickening, pericyte loss, ↑ permeability, capillary occlusion
    • → ischaemia.
ComplicationFeaturesScreening / management
Retinopathy
  • Background (microaneurysms, dot/blot haemorrhages, hard exudates) → pre-proliferative (cotton wool spots, venous beading, IRMA) → proliferative (neovascularisation → vitreous haemorrhage, retinal detachment)
  • Maculopathy (commonest cause of visual loss in T2DM)
  • Also cataracts, glaucoma
Annual retinal photography from age 12 (Diabetic Eye Screening Wales). Rx: glucose/BP control, laser photocoagulation, anti-VEGF injections (maculopathy), vitrectomy
NephropathyHyperfiltration → microalbuminuria (ACR ≥3) → overt proteinuria → ↓ eGFR → ESRD; Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules (nodular glomerulosclerosis); HTNAnnual urine ACR + eGFR. Rx: ACEi/ARB, SGLT2i, BP <130/80 if ACR >70, finerenone, glucose, statin
Neuropathy
  • Symmetrical distal sensory polyneuropathy (glove and stocking: loss of vibration, monofilament sensation, pain/burning)
  • Mononeuropathies (CN III with pupil sparing, carpal tunnel)
  • Amyotrophy
  • Autonomic (postural hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, bladder, gustatory sweating)
Annual foot check (10 g monofilament, pulses, skin). Rx: foot care/podiatry, neuropathic pain (amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, pregabalin), glucose control
  • Intensive glycaemic control reduces microvascular complications (UKPDS, DCCT); BP control is also crucial.

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of drugs used to treat type 2 diabetes and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
los.html:
DrugMechanismBenefitsSide effects / cautions
Metformin (biguanide)↓ hepatic gluconeogenesis, ↑ insulin sensitivity (AMPK)Weight neutral/↓, no hypos, CV benefit (UKPDS), cheapGI upset, lactic acidosis (avoid eGFR <30; review <45), B12 deficiency; stop with contrast/AKI
SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin)Block glucose reabsorption in PCT → glycosuria↓ HF hospitalisation, CV death, CKD progression, weight loss, ↓ BPGenital thrush, UTI, euglycaemic DKA, volume depletion, Fournier's gangrene (rare)
GLP-1 RAs (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide)Incretin: ↑ glucose-dependent insulin, ↓ glucagon, slow gastric emptying, ↓ appetiteWeight loss, CV benefit, no hyposGI (nausea), pancreatitis, gallstones; injection (oral semaglutide exists)
DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin, linagliptin)Block breakdown of endogenous GLP-1/GIPWeight neutral, no hypos, well toleratedPancreatitis (rare); modest efficacy
Sulfonylureas (gliclazide)Close β-cell K_ATP channels → ↑ insulin releaseCheap, effectiveHypoglycaemia, weight gain
Pioglitazone (TZD)PPAR-γ agonist → ↑ insulin sensitivityNo hyposFluid retention/HF, weight gain, fractures, bladder cancer
InsulinReplacementMost powerfulHypos, weight gain; injection technique, DVLA
Acarboseα-glucosidase inhibitorFlatulence
  • Choose by: CV/renal comorbidities (SGLT2i), weight (GLP-1 RA), hypoglycaemia risk (occupation, frailty), cost, patient preference.
